tracks.title: The second file
tracks.text: Lesson one point one — bundles. A sub-lesson, under the workbooks lesson… the one about the unit itself. The second file — that is the moment this lesson exists for. The parent lesson made you a one-file promise — the workbook is the app, the source, and the disk, in a single artifact. Then you ran the bundle command… and a second file appeared. Strange extension. Dot w-bundle. [curious] And every instinct you've trained on twenty years of software says — here it comes. The custom container. The moat. Those instincts are earned. Line up the famous offenders. The old dot doc — a proprietary binary dump… reverse-engineered, painfully. Dot p-s-d — a proprietary layered blob… opened partially, with heroics. Dot sketch — secretly a zip, schema undocumented for years. And then the w-bundle line reads differently — a zip, entries you already know… and it opens today, with unzip. So this lesson answers two questions, before anything else. Is this lock-in… and when I hand this file to someone — what exactly did I just hand them. Does my agent's memory go along for the ride?

tracks.title: It is a zip
tracks.text: The definition — and the relief. A w-bundle is a plain zip. The nineteen eighty-nine kind. Four entries inside, every one of them a standard older than most companies. First… workbook dot html. The runnable artifact — the app itself, rendered and self-contained. Second… workbook dot org. The source — prose, tasks, code — riding along so the recipient can re-author, not just run. Third… v-f-s dot sqlite. The project's disk, as plain SQLite — and it only comes along when the project actually has one. And fourth… manifest dot json. The label. One small object whose main job is to say — I am wbundle, version one. That defcard is not a summary of the spec. It is the spec. The runtime packs bundles with the zip library that ships in Erlang's standard library… the CLI packs them with a stock Rust zip crate. Two implementations. One deliberately boring container. [chuckles] Not a moat. A carton.

tracks.title: Open one with no Workbooks software
tracks.text: Next — open one, with no Workbooks software. Proof beats reassurance. So bundle a project… and crack the result open with the unzip command that has shipped on every Unix since before some of your dependencies were born. [excited] The listing comes back exactly as promised. Workbook dot html — the app… open it in a browser right now. Workbook dot org — the source. V-f-s dot sqlite — the disk. Manifest dot json — the label. [chuckles] Four compartments, one exploded carton — and one thesis stamped on it. The bundle is not the app… it is the shipping carton around the app. And it goes further than listing. The disk inside really is just a disk. The entire virtual file system is one SQLite table — volume, path, content, and a timestamp. Point the stock sqlite3 tool at it, select volume and path from vfs… and out comes the project's file listing, line by line — workspace, the orders data… workspace, the weekly report. With no Workbooks software installed. Anywhere. That's the no-moat moment. Every layer of the carton is inspectable with tooling you had before you ever heard of this project… the design promise of the whole anatomy, kept at the shipping layer too.

tracks.title: Bundle and unbundle
tracks.text: Next — bundle, and unbundle. The local round trip is two CLI verbs… both run entirely on your machine. No engine. No account. No network. First — how bundle decides what to pack. Hand it an org file directly. Or a directory — it looks for workbook dot org inside. Or a directory with exactly one org file — the obvious choice. Two or more candidates… it refuses. Name one, it says, or pass it explicitly. Guessing is not a feature in a packaging tool. Then the gate. Hand it unclean source and it refuses, verbatim — error… source has diagnostics — fix them first. [curious] Because a bundle is a thing you hand to other people. Once it's clean, picture a short conveyor. The source rolls in… hits the lint gate… a dirty file bounces off toward fix-them-first… a clean one rolls on to render — org becomes html — then to pack — a plain zip plus manifest — and out drops shop dot w-bundle. One last arrow, unbundle, runs the belt backward… unbundled shop dot w-bundle into shop — four files. The project back — org file, disk, rendered app. Not a flattened export. That's the difference between sending someone a printout… and sending them the document.

tracks.title: The smallest manifest in software
tracks.text: Now the label — possibly the smallest manifest in software. The whole thing fits on one line… six fields, read aloud. First… the id — the workbook's name. Second… the format tag — always wbundle slash one — the one tag both packing lanes emit. Third… volumes — which disk volumes made the trip. Fourth… signed — whether provenance travels with the bytes. Fifth… private underscore included — whether the privacy strip was skipped on purpose… more on that in a moment. And sixth… created — a unix timestamp. That's the whole label. No registry lookups. No nested config tree. Pack the same workbook on an engine instead, and the delta is small and legible — volumes now lists workspace, the one volume aboard. And there is exactly one field that ever appears conditionally — key refs, present only when entries are sealed. Read that one carefully. It's a reference… never a key. Which entry, which key id, which algorithm. The manifest tells you which door is locked and which keyring holds the key. The key itself never rides in the carton. Which is why a bundle — sealed entries and all — is safe to mirror to any storage you don't fully trust.

tracks.title: The same verbs at engine scale
tracks.text: Next — the same verbs, at engine scale. Everything so far ran on your laptop. The engine speaks the same container through two verbs of its own — ship packs a live workbook into a bundle blob… and restore is its exact inverse. And ship answers this lesson's opening worry. Before anything leaves the engine, the traveling disk copy gets stripped — one SQL statement, run against the egress copy. Delete from vfs… where the volume is not the workspace. Then vacuum. The disk has three named volumes… only one is public. First… workspace — the working tree, the work itself. Ships. Second… memory — the agent's long-term memory. Stays home. Third… tmp — scratch space. Stays home. Sharing exposes the work… never the session that produced it — enforced as a delete, not promised in a readme. Now the journey, end to end. The owner's engine strips, vacuums, and packs html, disk, and manifest into the carton — a plain zip, safe to mail, mirror, or archive. The recipient runs restore… and reopens the disk. The work — intact. One honest nuance. The engine's ship carries three entries to the CLI's four — an assembled workbook already embeds its source in the html. Same container. Same tag. Same restore.

tracks.title: One carton, every door
tracks.text: Next — one carton, every door. Here's what makes the boring container a design decision, not a missed opportunity. The platform reuses this exact zip shape for every flow where a workbook crosses a boundary. Picture a hub with five spokes — the w-bundle at the center, five doors fanning out. First — checkout and checkin. Pull a working tree down from an engine, or push edits back… the payload crossing the wire is this zip, wrapped in JSON. Second — store and fetch. Archiving a workbook is literally writing the blob to cold storage, under a key named after its slug. Third — publish. It accepts a w-bundle and pulls workbook dot html out of it, by name. Fourth — toolkit install. A built toolkit, compiled wasm and all, ships in the same container. The engine's own tests put it in writing… it's still just a w-bundle. And fifth — the fractal pack. A whole workspace — its index plus every member workbook — packs into one parent bundle. Containers hold containers. The carton nests. [excited] And the payoff of one shape everywhere — every tool that learns to open the carton learns every door at once. Including the tools that don't exist yet… and the ones that aren't ours.

tracks.title: The way back in, and the sealed case
tracks.text: Two more pieces of depth — the way back in… and when part of the carton is ciphertext. Plain zips have one classic ambush. An entry named dot dot, slash, dot dot, slash — hoping the extractor writes outside its target directory. [chuckles] The unbundler rejects any entry rooted at slash, or containing a dot-dot component. Refusing unsafe entry path in bundle, it says — and writes nothing. Now the sealed case. Sometimes a bundle should travel freely while part of it stays gated — a paid dataset inside a free demo. Ship can seal listed entries as real A-E-S two-fifty-six ciphertext, in an envelope you can audit. A seven-byte magic marker… a twelve-byte nonce… a sixteen-byte authentication tag… then the ciphertext. The keys never ride along. Each sealed entry gets its own fresh key — so revoking one doesn't unlock the rest — escrowed at the runtime. To open one, the client asks the engine to release the key… which runs the same access enforcement as any gated call. [curious] A wrong key, a tampered ciphertext, a mismatched context — all fail indistinguishably. The entry opens correctly… or not at all. A real gate is a key the client lacks. Not a login screen drawn over data.

tracks.title: Where the carton ends
tracks.text: Honesty section — where the carton ends. Five edges worth knowing before you lean on them. First… a bundle is a snapshot, not a replica. Nothing inside it syncs. If you want two copies to converge again, that's the engine's job — not the carton's. Second… bundle is not build. The bundle verb is local assembly — lint, render, zip. Compiling components is a different, engine-backed verb. Third… the two lanes differ by one entry — the CLI carries the org source as its own file, the engine doesn't need to. Fourth… sharing shares contents. Anyone can unzip what you send. That's the feature. The privacy strip protects the volumes that never left… sealed entries protect what shipped as ciphertext… everything else is readable by design. [exhales] Don't put a secret in the workspace and hope the extension protects it. And fifth — the html is still the artifact people open. The w-bundle is the shipping carton around it… it exists for round-tripping authorship, not viewing. Hand a reader the html. Hand a collaborator the carton. One last note — the engine packs with Erlang, the CLI with Rust… and the guarantee is the same container either way. Byte-identical archives are not the claim. Interchangeability is.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Questions people actually ask — quick fire. Can I just rename it to dot zip? [chuckles] Yes. It is one. The format is identified by the tag in the manifest, not by the file name. Why not just ship the bare html? You can — that's exactly what publish does. The bundle earns its keep when the recipient is a collaborator, not a viewer. Does my agent's memory ship when I share? Not from the engine, by default — the memory and scratch volumes are deleted from the egress copy before packing. And if you override that, the manifest says so… on the record. Will this open in twenty fifty-six? The carton is zip — in continuous use since nineteen eighty-nine. Inside it… html, SQLite, and U-T-F eight text. [curious] Pick the one you think dies first. The format's survival doesn't depend on this project existing — which is the strongest durability claim a format can make.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's the bundle. Not a format… a carton. A plain zip around the app, its source, and its disk — with a label so small you can recite it, a privacy strip that deletes the session before the work ships, and one shape reused at every door the engine has. The way back up is short. This page hangs off lesson one — workbooks, the unit. Everything here was just that lesson's one-file promise… kept while crossing a boundary. [curious] And if the disk inside the carton made you curious, the v-f-s lesson is where it lives in full. The carton carries. The parent lesson tells you what it's carrying… and why that thing was worth a format this boring.
